title: Y and en
description: Replace places, things and amounts with y and en, and put them in the right place.

guide.summary: Y and en are two short pronouns that swallow a whole phrase: y takes over à + a thing and any place, en takes over de + a thing, an amount and a counted noun. This topic also settles where they sit in the sentence.

sections.title: Y or en? Look at the little word in front
sections.text: Y and en replace the preposition together with its noun. Which one you need depends on that preposition, not on the meaning of the noun.

rows: je pense à mon examen → j’y pense
a place (à, dans, chez, en, sur)
il habite en France → il y habite
je parle du film → j’en parle
du, de la, de l’, des + noun
je veux du pain → j’en veux
a number or a quantity + noun
j’ai deux frères → j’en ai deux
lui, leur, à lui, de lui
je réponds à Marc → je lui réponds

steps: Find the phrase you want to replace and the word that introduces it.
À, or any preposition of place, gives y.
De, du, de la, des, or a number or quantity word, gives en.
Take the whole phrase away, preposition included.

examples.fr: Tu vas à la gare ? Oui, j’y vais.
examples.en: Are you going to the station? Yes, I’m going.

examples.fr: Du café ? J’en bois deux tasses par jour.
examples.en: Coffee? I drink two cups of it a day.

watch: The pronoun carries the preposition too: never j’y pense à mon examen.
The place word en (en France) is not the pronoun en; a place always gives y.
A person is different: see the people section.

sections.title: What y replaces
sections.text: Y stands for à + a thing or an idea, and for a place after any preposition of place.
steps: Ask what the phrase answers: where? or à what?
If it is a place, or à + a thing, replace the whole phrase with y.
Put y directly in front of the conjugated verb; je becomes j’ before it.

examples.en: She has worked there since May.

examples.fr: Nous y dînons à huit heures.
examples.en: We are having dinner there at eight.

watch: Chez Marc names a place, not a person: it gives y, never lui.
Au is à + le and aux is à + les, so they still count as à.
English often drops “there”; French never drops y.

sections.title: What en replaces
sections.text: En stands for de + a thing, and for an indefinite amount: du, de la, de l’, des + noun.

rows: elle est contente de son travail

steps: Check the preposition the verb or the adjective needs: parler de, avoir besoin de, être content de.
Ask whether the noun is “some” (du, de la, de l’, des) or a definite one (le, la, les).
De + a thing, or an indefinite amount, becomes en in front of the conjugated verb.

examples.fr: Elle en boit tous les matins.
Nous en avons besoin ce soir.

watch: Du café means some coffee; le café would be one particular coffee.
English can leave “some” out, but French still needs the pronoun.
Adjectives count too: content de, sûr de, fier de all lead to en.

sections.title: Counting: en takes the noun, the number stays
sections.text: When the noun is counted or measured, en replaces the noun alone. The number or quantity word stays after the verb, otherwise the sentence no longer says how many.

rows: nous voulons un kilo de tomates
il y a beaucoup de cafés
il y a + du / de la
il y a encore du gâteau
il n’y a pas de lait

steps: Replace only the noun (and its de) with en, never the amount.
Keep the number or quantity word after the verb, where the noun used to be.
With il y a, keep il y whole and slide en in just before a.

examples.fr: Des chaises ? Il y en a trois.
examples.en: Chairs? There are three of them.

watch: Never drop the amount: en on its own does not answer “how many”.
Y always comes before en, never the other way round.
“One” is une with a feminine noun and un with a masculine one.

sections.title: Where do y and en sit?
sections.text: Y and en stay glued to the verb they belong to. Nothing slips between the pronoun and that verb.

rows: j’y suis allé, j’en ai mangé
after the verb, with a hyphen
en goes between y and a

steps: Find the verb the phrase belongs to: the conjugated one, or the infinitive if it depends on that.
Put the pronoun directly in front of that verb; in the passé composé that means in front of the auxiliary.
Wrap ne before the pronoun and pas, jamais or plus after the verb.
Elide ne to n’ before y and en; the participle never agrees with en.

examples.en: I am going to go there.

watch: In a statement the pronoun never follows the verb: not il a en trois.
In the passé composé it stands before the auxiliary, not before the participle.
Only an affirmative command puts the pronoun after the verb, joined by a hyphen.

sections.title: People take other pronouns
sections.text: For a person, careful French does not use y or en. Most verbs with à take lui or leur before the verb; penser à and a few others keep à + a stressed pronoun; after de, a person keeps de + a stressed pronoun.

rows: je pense à lui / à elle

steps: Ask first whether you are replacing a thing or a person.
A thing after à gives y; a thing after de gives en.
A person after à normally gives lui or leur before the verb — but penser à keeps its à.
A person after de keeps de + moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles, after the verb.

examples.fr: Je réponds à ma sœur → je lui réponds.
examples.en: I answer my sister → I answer her.

examples.fr: Je pense à ma grand-mère → je pense à elle.
examples.en: I think about my grandmother → I think about her.

examples.fr: Nous parlons de notre voisine → nous parlons d’elle.
examples.en: We talk about our neighbour → we talk about her.

watch: Penser à never takes lui in front of the verb.
In everyday speech you will hear j’y pense and j’en parle about people too; here, practise the careful à lui, d’elle.
De + elle is written d’elle, and de + il does not exist: use the stressed forms.

sections.title: On y va, vas-y, allons-y
sections.text: A handful of everyday expressions keep y for good.

rows: on takes the il form: va
command: the pronoun follows, with a hyphen
go on, go ahead (to one friend)
va adds an s before y
this y belongs to the expression

steps: In a statement keep the pronoun in front of the verb: on y va.
In an affirmative command put it after the verb, joined by a hyphen.
Check the verb form: on takes the il form, and the tu command of aller gains an s before y.

examples.fr: Tout le monde est prêt ? On y va !

watch: Vas-y with an s, but allons-y and allez-y keep their normal forms.
Va-y and va-z-y are spoken slips, not written French.

steps: Ask “where?”: if the phrase answers it, it is a place.
Replace the preposition and the place together with y — à, dans, chez, en and sur all behave the same.
Put y directly in front of the conjugated verb, and shorten je to j’ before it.
Check the verb’s preposition: penser à, jouer à, répondre à all take à.
If what follows à is a thing or an idea, replace the whole à-phrase with y.
Remember that au is à + le and aux is à + les; they count as à.
Find the preposition the verb or the adjective needs: parler de, avoir besoin de, être content de.
If it is de, replace de + the noun with en.
Place en directly in front of the conjugated verb.
Ask whether the noun is “some” (du, de la, de l’, des) or a definite one (le, la, les).
An indefinite amount is replaced by en; a definite noun by le, la or les.
Keep the pronoun in front of the verb, even when English leaves the noun out.
Replace only the noun with en, and put en in front of the verb.
Leave the amount (deux, une, beaucoup, un kilo) after the verb, where the noun stood.
Make the counting word agree with the noun’s gender when it means “one”.
Keep il y a whole: its y never disappears.
Slide the pronoun for the noun in between y and a, and keep the amount after a.
Remember the order: y always comes first.
Build the pronoun + verb block first.
Put ne before the block, and pas, jamais or plus after the verb.
Elide ne to n’ before a pronoun starting with a vowel sound.
Decide which verb the phrase belongs to: the conjugated verb or the infinitive.
With a verb + infinitive, put the pronoun in front of the infinitive.
In the passé composé, put it in front of the auxiliary and leave the participle unchanged.
Ask whether what you replace is a person or a thing.
A thing after à gives y, a thing after de gives en.
A person after à usually gives lui or leur before the verb, but penser à keeps its preposition.
A person after de keeps de + a stressed pronoun after the verb.
In a statement, keep the pronoun in front of the verb.
In an affirmative command, put it after the verb with a hyphen.
Check the verb form: on takes the il form, and the tu command of aller gains an s before y.

exercises.source: Je vais à Paris demain.
exercises.hint: The pronoun goes directly before the conjugated verb, and je shortens before a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Take out à Paris entirely and put the pronoun before vais.
exercises.explanation: À Paris is a place introduced by à, so y replaces it and sits before vais: j’y vais demain.

mistakes.why: The pronoun has been left after the verb. In a statement it stands directly in front of the conjugated verb, and je is shortened before it.
The city is named twice: the pronoun already carries à Paris, so that phrase must disappear.
En replaces de + a noun or an amount. À Paris is a place introduced by à.
The position is right, but je cannot stay whole in front of a vowel sound; it needs its apostrophe form.

exercises.source: Il habite en France avec sa famille.
answers: Il y habite avec sa famille.
exercises.hint: Here en is a preposition of place, not the pronoun en.
exercises.feedback: Which pronoun stands for a place? It goes before habite.
exercises.explanation: Y replaces a place after any preposition of place (à, dans, chez, en, sur): il y habite avec sa famille.

answers: Il habite y avec sa famille.
mistakes.why: The pronoun is stranded after the verb. In a statement it comes in front of the conjugated verb.

answers: Il en habite avec sa famille.
mistakes.why: The en of en France is the preposition “in”, not the pronoun. A place calls for the place pronoun.

answers: Il y habite en France avec sa famille.
mistakes.why: The country is named twice. The pronoun already stands for en France, so the phrase has to go.

answers: Il habite en avec sa famille.
mistakes.why: This keeps the preposition and drops the country. A pronoun replaces preposition and noun together.

exercises.source: Elle travaille dans ce bureau ? Oui, elle ____ travaille depuis mai.
exercises.hint: Think about what dans ce bureau is.
exercises.feedback: The pronoun stands for a place introduced by dans.
exercises.explanation: Dans ce bureau is a place, so y replaces it: elle y travaille. En would replace de + noun; le and lui replace direct and indirect objects.

mistakes.why: En replaces de + a noun or a quantity, such as du café or deux livres. Dans ce bureau starts with dans, a preposition of place.
Le replaces a direct object with no preposition, and lui a person after à. Dans ce bureau is neither: it answers “where?”.

exercises.instruction: Write the pronoun that replaces chez Marc.
exercises.source: Nous dînons chez Marc ce soir. Nous ____ dînons à huit heures.
exercises.hint: Chez Marc means at Marc’s home.
exercises.feedback: Chez + a person names a place here, not the person.
exercises.explanation: Chez Marc is where we are having dinner, so it is a place and y replaces it: nous y dînons.

mistakes.why: En stands for de + a noun or an amount. Chez Marc is introduced by chez, a preposition of place.
Lui replaces a person after à, the one you speak or answer to. Marc is not the guest here: his home is where the dinner happens.
Le replaces a direct object with no preposition, like le dîner. The phrase to replace answers “where?”.
Là is an adverb and comes after the verb (nous dînons là). The blank sits in front of the verb, a slot only a pronoun fills.

exercises.source: She lives there. (there = in Lyon)

alternatives.message: That is correct French, but this exercise asks for the pronoun y before the verb: elle y habite.
That is correct French, but this exercise asks for the pronoun y before the verb: elle y vit.
That is correct French, but this exercise asks for the pronoun y before the verb: elle y habite.
That is correct French, but this exercise asks for the pronoun y before the verb: elle y vit.

exercises.hint: Use habiter or vivre; the pronoun comes before the verb.
exercises.feedback: Put the pronoun for the place before the verb, not after it.
exercises.explanation: In Lyon is a place, so y replaces it before the verb: elle y habite.

mistakes.why: The pronoun has been left after the verb. In French it stands in front of the conjugated verb.
En replaces de + a noun or an amount, not a place after à. In Lyon answers “where?”.
The city is named twice: the pronoun already carries à Lyon, so the place must not come back.
Dedans means “inside”, about a container. A town reached with à is carried by a short pronoun before the verb.

exercises.instruction: Replace à mon examen with y.
exercises.source: Je pense à mon examen.
exercises.hint: Penser à + a thing: which pronoun replaces à + a thing?
exercises.feedback: Remove à mon examen and put the pronoun before pense; remember that je elides.
exercises.explanation: Y replaces à + a thing or an idea: je pense à mon examen → j’y pense.

mistakes.why: The pronoun is left after the verb. It belongs immediately in front of the conjugated verb.
En replaces de + a noun. Penser takes à when it means thinking about something, so nothing here starts with de.
The exam is named twice. The pronoun already stands for à mon examen.
The pronoun is in the right place, but je must be shortened in front of a vowel sound.

exercises.source: Vous répondez à ce message ? Oui, nous ____ répondons ce soir.
exercises.hint: Répondre à + a thing, not a person.
exercises.feedback: A message is a thing, and it comes after à.
exercises.explanation: Répondre à + a thing becomes y: nous y répondons. Lui would replace à + a person; le and en do not replace à.

mistakes.why: En replaces de + a noun or an amount. Répondre is followed by à, not by de.
Lui stands for a person after à, the one you answer to. What is answered here is ce message, a thing.
Le replaces a direct object that follows the verb with no preposition. Répondre needs à before its object.

exercises.instruction: Write the pronoun that replaces au tennis.
exercises.source: Il joue au tennis le samedi. Il ____ joue avec son frère.
exercises.hint: Au is à + le. What replaces à + a thing?
exercises.feedback: The pronoun must stand for à + a game.
exercises.explanation: Jouer à + a game: au tennis is à + le tennis, so y replaces it: il y joue avec son frère.

mistakes.why: En replaces de + a noun or a quantity. Jouer à un sport uses à: au is à + le.
Le replaces a direct object with no preposition. The sport here arrives after à.
Lui replaces a person after à, not a game. Tennis is a thing.
Au is the preposition itself (à + le). A pronoun must replace the whole phrase, preposition included, not repeat part of it.

exercises.source: Mon travail ? J’en pense tous les jours.
answers: Mon travail ? J’y pense tous les jours.
exercises.hint: Which preposition follows penser when you think about something?
exercises.feedback: Penser takes à, not de, in this meaning.
exercises.explanation: Penser à quelque chose: à + a thing gives y, so j’y pense. En would need de.

answers: Mon travail ? J’en pense tous les jours.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged. En replaces de + a noun, and penser de is not how French says you think about something.

answers: Mon travail ? Je pense à lui tous les jours.
Je pense à lui tous les jours.
mistakes.why: À lui is kept for a person. Un travail is a thing, so it takes the pronoun for à + a thing.

answers: Mon travail ? Je y pense tous les jours.
Je y pense tous les jours.
mistakes.why: The pronoun is now the right one, but je keeps no e in front of a vowel sound; it needs its apostrophe form.

exercises.instruction: Replace de mon voyage with en.
exercises.source: Je parle de mon voyage.
exercises.hint: Parler de + a thing.
exercises.feedback: Remove the whole of de mon voyage and put the pronoun before parle; je elides.
exercises.explanation: En replaces de + a thing: je parle de mon voyage → j’en parle.

mistakes.why: The pronoun is stranded after the verb. It belongs directly in front of the conjugated verb.
Y stands for à + a thing or a place. Parler takes de before its topic.
The trip is named twice. The pronoun already contains de mon voyage.
The position is right, but je must be shortened before a vowel sound; je en is never written.

exercises.source: Vous avez besoin de la voiture ? Oui, nous ____ avons besoin ce soir.
exercises.hint: Look at the preposition in avoir besoin de.
exercises.feedback: Avoir besoin is followed by de.
exercises.explanation: Avoir besoin de + a thing: de la voiture becomes en, so nous en avons besoin. La would replace a direct object without de.

mistakes.why: Y replaces à + a thing or a place. Avoir besoin is built with de.
La and le replace a direct object that follows the verb with no preposition. Here the noun arrives after de, which they cannot swallow.

exercises.instruction: Write the pronoun that replaces de son travail.
exercises.source: Elle est contente de son travail. Elle ____ est très contente.
exercises.hint: Être content de + a thing.
exercises.feedback: The adjective content is followed by de.
exercises.explanation: Être content de quelque chose: de + a thing becomes en, so elle en est très contente.

mistakes.why: Y replaces à + a thing or a place. The adjective contente is followed by de.
La replaces a feminine direct object with no preposition, and it would leave the de stranded.
Le replaces a masculine direct object with no preposition. The phrase to replace is de son travail, preposition included.
De on its own is the preposition, not a pronoun. The blank needs the pronoun that stands for de + the noun.

exercises.source: Ce livre ? Elle y parle souvent.
answers: Ce livre ? Elle en parle souvent.
exercises.hint: Parler takes which preposition before the topic?
exercises.feedback: Parler de: the pronoun must replace de + a thing.
exercises.explanation: You talk de quelque chose, so the pronoun is en: elle en parle souvent.

answers: Ce livre ? Elle y parle souvent.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged. Y is for à + a thing or a place, and parler à points at the listener, not at the topic.

answers: Ce livre ? Elle le parle souvent.
mistakes.why: Parler le only works for languages (elle parle le russe). Talking about something uses parler de.

answers: Ce livre ? Elle parle en souvent.
mistakes.why: The pronoun has been moved behind the verb. It always stands in front of the conjugated verb.

exercises.source: Je veux du pain.
exercises.hint: Du pain is a partitive: some bread.
exercises.feedback: Le would mean one specific loaf. Use the pronoun for an amount of something.
exercises.explanation: En replaces a partitive noun (du, de la, de l’, des + noun): je veux du pain → j’en veux.

mistakes.why: The pronoun has been left after the verb; it belongs in front of it.
Le points at one particular loaf (le pain). Du pain is an amount of bread.
Y replaces à + a thing or a place. Du pain begins with du, which is de + le.
The bread is named twice. The pronoun already stands for du pain.
The pronoun is placed correctly, but je is shortened before a vowel sound; je en is not written.

exercises.source: Elle boit du café le matin ? Oui, elle ____ boit tous les matins.
exercises.hint: Is du café a specific coffee or some coffee?
exercises.feedback: A partitive noun is not replaced by le or la.
exercises.explanation: Du café is partitive, so en replaces it: elle en boit. Le would replace a definite noun such as le café.

mistakes.why: Le and la point at one definite thing, the coffee you already know about. Du café means some coffee, an amount.
Y replaces à + a thing or a place. Du café is an amount, introduced by du = de + le.

exercises.instruction: Write the pronoun that replaces des légumes.
exercises.source: Nous mangeons des légumes. Nous ____ mangeons à chaque repas.
exercises.hint: Des légumes means some vegetables.
exercises.feedback: Des + noun is replaced by the same pronoun as du and de la.
exercises.explanation: Des légumes is an indefinite plural, which en replaces: nous en mangeons à chaque repas.

mistakes.why: Les points at particular vegetables already known. Des légumes means some vegetables, an indefinite amount.
Y replaces à + a thing or a place. Des légumes is an amount and starts with des.
Des is the article you started from, not a pronoun. The blank needs the pronoun that replaces des + the noun.
Le is singular and definite. The noun here is plural and indefinite, so a definite pronoun does not fit.

exercises.instruction: Replace des fruits with a pronoun and build the sentence.
exercises.source: Elle achète des fruits au marché.
exercises.hint: Des fruits means some fruit; it is not a definite noun.
exercises.feedback: Les replaces a definite plural such as les fruits. Choose the pronoun for des.
exercises.explanation: Des fruits is indefinite, so en replaces it before achète; au marché stays where it is.

mistakes.why: Les stands for particular fruit already mentioned (les fruits). Des fruits is an indefinite amount.
The pronoun has been dropped behind the verb. It stands in front of the conjugated verb.
Two problems: les is for definite fruit already known, and a pronoun never sits after the conjugated verb in a statement.

exercises.source: Do you want some? (some = soup; to a friend)
exercises.hint: Some soup is a partitive in French; the pronoun goes before veux.
exercises.feedback: English some has no noun here, but French still needs a pronoun before the verb.
exercises.explanation: Some soup is de la soupe, a partitive, so en replaces it: tu en veux ?

mistakes.why: The pronoun is missing. English can say “do you want?” with nothing after it, but French needs a pronoun in front of the verb to carry “some”.
Le points at one definite thing. Some soup is an amount, de la soupe, not a particular object.
The pronoun has been left at the end. It must stand directly in front of the verb.
Y replaces à + a thing or a place. Soup here is an amount, introduced by de la.
That names the soup again instead of replacing it; the task is to use a pronoun.

exercises.instruction: Replace frères with en and keep the number.
exercises.source: J’ai deux frères.
exercises.hint: The number does not disappear; it stays after the verb.
exercises.feedback: Put the pronoun before ai and leave deux at the end.
exercises.explanation: With a number, en replaces the noun and the number stays at the end: j’en ai deux.

mistakes.why: The number is there but the pronoun is missing, so nothing says two of what.
The noun has stayed. The pronoun already stands for frères, so only the number remains.
The pronoun has slipped behind the verb. It stands in front of the conjugated verb, and only the amount follows.
The number has been dropped. With a counted noun the amount always stays at the end.
Les points at particular brothers already known, and it cannot be combined with a number this way.

exercises.source: Combien de livres as-tu ? (three)
exercises.hint: Which pronoun goes with a number, and where does it sit?
exercises.feedback: The pronoun goes before the verb; the number goes after it.
exercises.explanation: En replaces livres and the number trois stays after the verb: j’en ai trois.

mistakes.why: The pronoun has been put after the verb. Object pronouns stand in front of the conjugated verb, and only the amount follows.
Les points at definite books already mentioned, and it cannot be combined with a number this way.
Y replaces à + a thing or a place. Counting books calls for the pronoun that stands for de + a noun.

exercises.source: Tu as une voiture ? Oui, j’en ai ____.
exercises.hint: With en, the quantity stays after the verb. Voiture is feminine.
exercises.feedback: Keep the number from the question; do not drop it.
exercises.explanation: Une counts the car, so it stays at the end: j’en ai une.

mistakes.why: That is the masculine form. Voiture is feminine, so the counting word at the end must match it.
Writing the noun again undoes the pronoun: the pronoun before the verb already stands for the car, so only the amount belongs at the end.
En already stands in front of the verb. The blank holds the amount, which answers “how many”.
La is a definite pronoun, not a quantity, and it cannot sit at the end of the sentence.

exercises.source: Des enfants ? Ils ont en trois.
answers: Des enfants ? Ils en ont trois.
exercises.hint: Where do object pronouns go?
exercises.feedback: The pronoun belongs before the conjugated verb; only the number follows it.
exercises.explanation: En goes before ont and trois stays at the end: ils en ont trois.

answers: Des enfants ? Ils ont en trois.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged: the pronoun is still behind the verb, where an object pronoun never goes.

answers: Des enfants ? Ils en ont trois enfants.
mistakes.why: The noun has come back. The pronoun already stands for enfants, so only the number stays.
The number has been dropped. With a counted noun the amount must stay at the end.

answers: Des enfants ? Ils les ont trois.
mistakes.why: Les points at definite children already known and cannot be combined with a number this way.

exercises.instruction: Replace de tomates with a pronoun, keep un kilo, and build the sentence.
exercises.source: Nous voulons un kilo de tomates.
exercises.hint: The quantity un kilo stays after the verb.
exercises.feedback: Replace the de + noun part and keep the amount at the end.
exercises.explanation: After a quantity word, de tomates becomes en and un kilo stays: nous en voulons un kilo.

mistakes.why: Without a pronoun the sentence no longer says a kilo of what: the tomatoes have vanished.
Les stands for definite tomatoes already known, and it cannot introduce an amount.
The pronoun has been placed after the verb. It belongs in front of the conjugated verb, with the amount after it.

exercises.instruction: Replace chaises with en and keep the number.
exercises.source: Il y a trois chaises dans la cuisine.
answers: Il y en a trois dans la cuisine.
exercises.hint: Il y a is fixed; the new pronoun goes between y and a.
exercises.feedback: Keep il y together and put the pronoun just before a.
exercises.explanation: Il y a + a quantity becomes il y en a + the quantity: il y en a trois dans la cuisine.

answers: Il y a trois dans la cuisine.
mistakes.why: Nothing says three of what. Il y a + a number still needs a pronoun for the noun you removed.

answers: Il en a trois dans la cuisine.
mistakes.why: The y of il y a has gone, and il en a means “he has”. The expression keeps its y.

answers: Il y en a trois chaises dans la cuisine.
mistakes.why: The noun is still there. The pronoun already stands for chaises, so only the number remains.

answers: Il en y a trois dans la cuisine.
mistakes.why: The two pronouns are the wrong way round: y always comes first.

exercises.source: Il reste du gâteau ? Oui, il ____ a encore.
exercises.hint: Two pronouns meet here; one of them belongs to il y a.
exercises.feedback: Keep the y of il y a and add the pronoun for du gâteau in the right order.
exercises.explanation: Il y a keeps its y, and en replaces du gâteau; y always comes before en: il y en a encore.

mistakes.why: The order is reversed. When the two meet, y always comes first.
That keeps only the y of il y a and says nothing about the cake. A second pronoun is needed for du gâteau.
That drops the y of il y a, and il en a would mean “he has some”. The expression keeps its own y.

exercises.row: il y a + du / de la

exercises.source: Des cafés dans ta rue ? Il y ____ a beaucoup.
exercises.hint: Beaucoup is a quantity.
exercises.feedback: A quantity at the end needs a pronoun for the noun.
exercises.explanation: En replaces cafés and beaucoup stays at the end: il y en a beaucoup.

mistakes.why: The y of il y a is already printed in the sentence. The blank holds the pronoun for the cafés.
Les is a definite pronoun and cannot follow the y here. Beaucoup counts an indefinite amount.
Des is the article you started from, not a pronoun. The blank needs the pronoun that replaces des + the noun.

exercises.source: There are two of them. (them = banks)

exercises.source: Tu penses souvent à ta grand-mère ? Oui, je pense souvent ____.

exercises.feedback: Y replaces things and places. After penser à, a person needs à + a stressed pronoun.

exercises.instruction: Replace de Paul with a pronoun, in careful French.

exercises.instruction: Write the pronoun that replaces à ta sœur.

Répondre à is not one of the verbs that keep their preposition with a person; it takes an indirect-object pronoun before the verb.

exercises.instruction: Fix the pronoun for careful French: the teacher is a person.

exercises.source: We often talk about her. (her = our neighbour)

In careful French en replaces things. For a person, keep de and use elle: on parle souvent d’elle.
